strengths: Addresses critical legal and regulatory barriers to open LLM research with concrete real-world impact demonstrated through adoption by Anthropic and multiple European labs
Largest explicitly permissively-licensed/public domain multilingual dataset at 2 trillion tokens with detailed provenance, comprehensive metadata, and adherence to open data best practices
Thoughtful data curation including OCRonos correction, toxicity filtering via Celadon classifier, PII removal, and development of useful open-source tools
Strong motivation grounded in concrete examples of dataset takedowns (Books3, LAION, MATH) that harm reproducible research
Extensive documentation and transparent discussion of limitations including the 'open data paradox', supporting future responsible data collection efforts
weaknesses: Fundamentally a technical report rather than research paper—combines existing techniques (OCR, filtering, curation) with no novel methodology, algorithms, or theoretical contributions suitable for top-tier research venue

Severely underevaluated: no systematic quality comparison with C4C/KL3M/Common Pile, no controlled experiments demonstrating performance improvements, and no evidence models trained on this data outperform alternatives
Overclaimed as 'largest'—2T tokens is comparable to KL3M (1.2T) and Common Pile (1T), far below the 14-36T tokens used by state-of-the-art models; ethical compliance claims lack legal review

Technical soundness concerns: OCRoscope achieves only 59% quality vs. French National Library's 85%; Celadon toxicity filter trained on 2M samples lacks published precision/recall metrics; license verification process (Appendix C) is ad-hoc with potential jurisdictional biases

Insufficient for claimed use cases: dataset is 57% public domain (historical content with limited modern relevance), authors acknowledge it is 'far from covering the whole range of available resources', and explicitly inadequate for large model training

Impact evidence is anecdotal with redacted/vague model names and unsubstantiated performance claims; Section 5 mentions 'currently leading evaluations' without any published benchmarks or reproducible results
Multilingual claims overstated—English comprises 48.5% of tokens; authors admit low-resource language coverage remains 'still shallow' and distribution heavily skewed by web source dominance

strengths: Addresses an important, timely problem: the open data paradox and legal/ethical constraints on LLM training data
Comprehensive documentation with excellent provenance tracking and metadata across six collections and multiple languages
Broader multilingual coverage than most competing open datasets (50+ languages vs. English-focused alternatives)
Thoughtful consideration of ethical concerns: copyright verification, GDPR/PII removal, toxicity filtering
Evidence of practical adoption by industry (Anthropic) and research institutions demonstrates real-world utility
weaknesses: CRITICAL: No empirical evaluation of dataset quality or performance. No comparison of models trained on Common Corpus vs. alternatives (C4, Dolma, RefinedWeb) on standard benchmarks. Third-party usage mentioned but no controlled experiments.

CRITICAL: Curation components (OCRonos, Celadon toxicity filter, PII removal) are not rigorously evaluated. No false positive/negative rates, no ablation studies, no validation that filtering actually improves downstream performance.

Very limited technical novelty: aggregation of existing sources + application of standard techniques (fine-tuned LLM for OCR correction, DeBERTa classifier for toxicity). No novel methods or algorithmic contributions.

No comparative analysis with competing open datasets. Doesn't explain what is novel about Common Corpus vs. Dolma (3T tokens), C4C, KL3M, Common Pile. No head-to-head comparison on diversity, quality, or downstream task performance.

Incomplete scope and understated limitations: acknowledges not covering 'whole range of available open data' (never quantified), explicitly states low-resource language coverage is 'still shallow', and 2T tokens insufficient for largest modern models (14-36T). Dataset unsuitable for instruction-tuning and specialized tasks.

Missing statistical rigor: token counts reported without confidence intervals or quality metrics. OCRoscope achieves 59% OCR quality—is this acceptable? No thresholds or comparisons. No inter-annotator agreement for Celadon toxicity labeling.

Reproducibility concerns: tools described as 'released as parts of separate work' with unclear availability. Full dataset accessibility to reviewers not guaranteed. No commitment to permanent archival.

Impact section (Section 5) conflates adoption with validation. Mentions models using Common Corpus but provides no evidence they outperform alternatives. Claims about RAG model 'leading evaluations' are unsubstantiated.
Presentation issues: Figure 1 (world map) is difficult to interpret, Figure 2b (t-SNE) provides no clear insight, many critical details relegated to 50+ page appendices.

Methodological concerns inadequately addressed: OCRonos described as operating as 'synthetic rewriting tool'—could corrupt semantic meaning. PII replacement with 'fictitious but realistic values' could introduce spurious patterns. No discussion of side effects.

strengths: Addresses critical infrastructure need: tackles the 'open data paradox' and provides 2 trillion tokens of legally compliant open pre-training data, addressing growing copyright concerns and regulatory constraints
Exceptional documentation and transparency: comprehensive provenance documentation, license tracking, and data source details exemplify best practices for responsible dataset release
Meaningful multilingual coverage: provides substantial coverage of multiple European languages (top 9 languages have 10B+ tokens each), filling a gap in open multilingual datasets

Demonstrated real-world adoption: concrete evidence of impact with 7 European SLMs trained on Common Corpus as of May 2025, including from leading institutions (Anthropic, Barcelona Supercomputing Center)
Comprehensive curation infrastructure: developed specialized tools (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRonos, Celadon) to handle domain-specific challenges in historical texts and quality control
Thoughtful ethical considerations: explicitly addresses PII removal, toxicity detection across multiple bias dimensions, and transparent licensing practices
weaknesses: Lack of systematic dataset quality evaluation: no comparative analysis against other open datasets (C4C, KL3M, Common Pile) on text quality, diversity, or domain coverage metrics

No downstream task evaluation: missing critical validation that models trained on Common Corpus perform competitively with models trained on other open datasets; no controlled experiments with standard benchmarks

Unvalidated curation choices: toxicity filtering (Celadon) and OCR correction (OCRonos) lack empirical validation of quality and false positive/negative rates; no ablation studies showing impact on model performance
Limited technical novelty: tools are straightforward applications of existing techniques (DeBERTa, Llama 3); primarily an engineering/curation contribution rather than methodological innovation

Incomplete scope addressing of acknowledged limitations: corpus is incomplete by design ('open data paradox'), low-resource language coverage is shallow, 2 trillion tokens is 'suitable for models of limited size' only, lacks instruction-tuning data

Reproducibility concerns: dataset volatility (sources may be taken down), deduplication procedures unclear, language identification via fastText without error analysis, Anthropic work details redacted
Methodological gaps in validation: no inter-annotator agreement for subjective decisions, OCRoscope reports 59% quality rate without adequate discussion, sparse statistical analysis of claims

strengths: Addresses a timely and critical problem: legal/ethical concerns around LLM pre-training data are increasingly impeding open science research with concrete examples (NYT v. OpenAI, Books3, GEITje takedowns)

Large-scale, carefully curated dataset (~2 trillion tokens) that is unique in combining multilingual coverage, non-web sources, and strict permissive licensing; satisfies all four criteria from Table 1 simultaneously
Comprehensive documentation with detailed provenance for each collection, clear metadata structure, language distribution, and token counts enabling reproducibility and reusability
Multilingual diversity spanning 50+ languages including low-resource varieties (Maltese, Estonian, Lithuanian) with 9 languages having 10B+ tokens
Useful tools released as Bad Data Toolbox (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) addressing real challenges with OCR'd and historical data
Proper attention to ethical considerations: GDPR compliance, PII removal, toxicity filtering, and alignment with open science best practices
Document-level quality evaluation across 300K samples with multiple metrics and good corpus-level analysis with temporal/semantic visualizations
weaknesses: Weak model evaluation undermines claims of utility: only two small models trained with average (not superior) performance; 350M model smaller than baselines making comparisons unfair; results on XStoryCloze/XCOPA are merely comparable to baselines

No downstream task evaluation: limited to linguistic probes (MultiBLIMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA); no fine-tuning experiments, QA, summarization, translation, or other tasks demonstrating practical utility

Critical scale limitation: 2 trillion tokens acknowledged as suitable only up to 1.2B parameters; modern models require 14-36 trillion tokens, severely limiting impact and making dataset inadequate for competitive model training
Limited technical novelty: primarily an aggregation and curation effort building on existing sources (OpenAlex, The Stack, Internet Archive) rather than proposing new technical methods or insights

Data quality concerns inadequately addressed: (1) OCRonos can perform 'synthetic rewriting' on degraded content risking semantic drift; (2) Celadon toxicity filtering relies on synthetic LLM annotations not validated against human judgment; (3) PII replacement with 'fictitious realistic values' potential artifacts unexplored; (4) deduplication reported as 'negligible' without actual percentages

Unresolved 'open data paradox': paper identifies that major open sources are 'paradoxically little visible online' but doesn't overcome this; acknowledges incomplete coverage of available open resources
Incomplete coverage: web archives excluded (deferred to future), Open Science collection 85% English, no instruction-tuning data; dataset doesn't cover full range of available open data

Insufficient analysis and reproducibility: no investigation of which data sources drive model performance; missing ablations; toxicity filtering thresholds not specified; no human evaluation of cleaned data; no analysis of temporal biases in historical OCR'd text
Missing critical comparisons: no direct performance comparison with models trained on Common Pile, KL3M, or Dolma; only two curated baselines examined (Gemma 3, OLMo)

strengths: Addresses a timely need for copyright-compliant pre-training data, with strong motivation around reproducibility and legal sustainability
Extensive documentation of data provenance, sources, and curation procedures aligned with dataset best practices
Multilingual coverage across 50+ languages with meaningful token counts, not restricted to high-resource languages
Released curation tools (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) with potential community utility
Large-scale assembly effort producing 2 trillion tokens from legally compliant sources with transparent source attribution
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only two small models (350M, 1.2B) trained on different data budgets; results show 'comparable' rather than superior performance compared to baselines (e.g., 0.774 vs 0.762 on MultiBLiMP), which is weak evidence of dataset quality

Curation tool quality unsubstantiated: OCRoscope estimates 59% quality for text institutions claim is 85% clean; OCRerrcr and OCRonos lack rigorous evaluation and human validation; no ablation studies quantifying impact of filtering steps
Dataset size (2T tokens) is modest by 2025 standards; authors acknowledge suitability only for small models, severely limiting practical utility compared to 14-36T token modern datasets

Fundamental lack of technical novelty: this is data aggregation using standard techniques (OCR, toxicity filtering, deduplication), not methodological contribution; reads as technical report rather than research paper

No head-to-head experimental comparison with related work (Common Pile, KL3M, Dolma); critical missing experiment is training equivalent models on Common Corpus vs. alternatives to demonstrate relative quality

Insufficient evaluation rigor: only three dated benchmarks (MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA); no downstream task evaluation; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; no analysis of dataset strengths/weaknesses per language or domain

Incomplete coverage undermines comprehensiveness claims: Open Web limited to 4 sources; Creative Commons web data unresolved; Open Science 85% English; 'open data paradox' invoked but not rigorously investigated

Concerns about data quality not addressed: toxicity classifier performance on historical OCR'd text unclear; PII replacement with 'fictitious values' could introduce artifacts; no human evaluation of actual quality across collections

Missing critical ablations and analysis: no quantification of filtering step impacts, no language-specific analysis, no investigation of what makes Common Corpus distinct beyond licensing, no guidance for practitioners on when to use it vs. alternatives

Reproducibility limitations: while provenance documented, actually reproducing the dataset construction could be challenging; tool repositories mentioned but not clearly linked in main text; single experimental runs with no confidence bounds reported

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem of legal compliance and open science in LLM pre-training with a concrete large-scale solution
Exceptionally thorough documentation of provenance, licensing, languages, and composition exceeding best practices for dataset papers
Substantial multilingual coverage across 50+ languages with at least 10B tokens for 9 languages, differentiating from English-centric datasets
Releases multiple open-source tools (Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Celadon) with independent value for data curation
Demonstrates responsible data practices through OCR correction, PII removal, toxicity filtering, and deduplication
Validates dataset utility by training models and evaluating on multiple benchmarks (MultiBLIMP, XStoryCloze, XCOPA)
weaknesses: Limited empirical validation: Table 2 shows 'comparable' performance, not superior—the 350M model achieves only marginal improvements on MultiBLIMP and underperforms on other benchmarks, failing to demonstrate technical advantage
No direct comparative evaluation—missing the critical experiment of training identical models on Common Corpus vs. FineWeb/C4 at equal scale to establish value proposition

Data quality claims lack rigorous support: curation tools have acknowledged accuracy limitations (OCRoscope 59-85%, OCRonos synthetic rewriting), not validated on final corpus; Celadon applied but final dataset not audited

Overstated claims: title claims 'ethical data' (primarily legal compliance), 'largest collection' (outdated—current models train on 14-36T tokens), and 'outstanding performance' on MultiBLIMP (0.774 vs 0.762 is marginal)
Limited novelty: primarily a curation and aggregation effort using standard techniques (license filtering, OCR correction, PII removal); no methodological innovations

Insufficient evaluation scope: only three narrow benchmarks tested, no downstream tasks (classification, generation, reasoning); fastText language ID suboptimal; per-language quality not systematically evaluated despite multilingual claims
Language representation heavily skewed (49% English) undermines 'multilingual' positioning; only 9 languages have 10B+ tokens despite 50+ language claim
Reproducibility gaps: reconstruction instructions not explicit, filtering decisions appear arbitrary (75% digits threshold), deduplication marked 'negligible' without detailed analysis
No analysis of performance-compliance trade-off: unclear whether legal compliance requirements reduce model capability relative to larger uncurated datasets
